grammar.title: 不客气 for "you're welcome"
grammar.explanation: 不客气 (bú kèqi) is the standard reply to 谢谢 ("thank you"), similar to "you're welcome" or "don't mention it". Literally it means "don't be (so) polite".

grammar.title: 对不起 and 没什么
grammar.pattern: 对不起 (apology) / 没什么 (it's nothing)
grammar.explanation: 对不起 (duìbuqǐ) means "I'm sorry" or "excuse me", used to apologize or get someone's attention. 没什么 (méi shénme) is a common reply meaning "it's nothing" or "no big deal".

grammar.title: 很 + adjective for descriptions
grammar.explanation: 很 (hěn) goes right before an adjective used as the predicate, since Chinese adjectives don't need a separate "to be" verb. Even when it isn't emphasizing "very", 很 is often still included just to sound natural — an adjective alone can sound like an unfinished comparison. Never add 是 before the adjective.

grammar.title: 没关系 for "it's OK"
grammar.explanation: 没关系 (méi guānxi) means "it doesn't matter" or "no worries" — a common reply when someone apologizes or worries about causing trouble. It pairs naturally with 对不起.

grammar.title: 呢 for follow-up questions
grammar.explanation: After stating something, 你呢? asks "and you?" without repeating the whole sentence. 呢 (ne) attaches to the topic being asked about and relies on context from what was just said.

grammar.title: 请问 for "excuse me, may I ask"
grammar.explanation: 请问 (qǐngwèn) politely opens a question, similar to "Excuse me, ..." or "May I ask...". It always comes first, before the actual question.
